strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: post-training quantization specifically tailored to DiT-based Real-ISR, which differs from both U-Net SR quantization and generic text-to-image DiT quantization due to sensitivity to fine textures.

The three components (H-SVD, VaSMP, VaTMP) are each grounded in clear motivating analyses (PCA of principal components in Fig. 4, layer-wise weight variance heterogeneity in Fig. 5, temporal activation variance trends in Fig. 6) and simple rate-distortion derivations, giving the design choices a principled flavor rather than being purely heuristic.

Extensive empirical validation: four real-world benchmarks, both W4A6 and W4A4 settings, comparison against 9 competitive baselines spanning diffusion-specific, DiT-specific, and SR-specific quantization methods, plus PEFT-based quantization baselines.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (Tables 2-4), plus additional analyses on artifact localization (ROI-PSNR, Edge MAE, Color MAE in Table 9), calibration-set robustness (Table 8), and backbone generalization to DreamClear (Table 7).

Practical efficiency numbers are reported (peak memory, end-to-end speedup, runtime breakdown), and the paper discusses implementation details (parallel branch execution, Triton kernel for the local SVD branch) that lend credibility to the claimed speedups.
The limitations section is candid, acknowledging remaining W4A4 artifacts and the lack of native arbitrary-precision kernel support, rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The core techniques build heavily on established building blocks (Hadamard incoherence processing from QuaRot/RobuQ, low-rank branch idea from SVDQuant, rate-distortion-based bit allocation similar to HAWQ-style approaches); the primary novelty is the block-wise rank-1 local SVD component and its application-specific instantiation for spatio-temporal precision scheduling, which is a comparatively incremental extension.

Generalization evidence to a second backbone (DreamClear) is limited to a single table (Table 7) on one dataset (RealSR) without ablations of the individual modules on that backbone, leaving the claimed backbone-agnosticism only lightly supported.

Some baseline results appear extremely weak (e.g., QueST MUSIQ ~37-45 vs. FP ~65-72, PassionSR/Q-Diffusion producing near-random LIQE scores), raising a question about whether these baselines were adequately adapted/tuned for the DiT4SR backbone and SR task, which could inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

The W4A6 DreamClear result where quantized MUSIQ/MANIQA/ClipIQA notably exceed FP performance is explained only speculatively ("mild perceptual regularizer"), which is not rigorously verified and could instead reflect known unreliability of no-reference IQA metrics under distribution shift from quantization noise, undermining confidence in some reported gains.

The theoretical derivations for VaSMP/VaTMP rely on several simplifying assumptions (Gaussian per-token/per-channel statistics after Hadamard transform, shared uniform quantizer distortion model across heterogeneous layer types) that are not independently validated beyond qualitative variance plots, and the greedy discretization/DP procedures are heuristic approximations to the underlying combinatorial allocation problem without optimality guarantees.

Hardware/setup for latency profiling (RTX 4090) differs from the main calibration/evaluation hardware (RTX A6000) without justification, and no statistical variance (e.g., multiple seeds/crops) is reported for quantitative results, limiting reproducibility confidence.
Code and models are stated as "will be available" rather than released, so reproducibility cannot be currently verified by reviewers.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR models, which is underexplored compared to U-Net quantization or generic DiT quantization for text-to-image tasks. The paper convincingly demonstrates (via Fig. 2 and 4) that existing generic DiT quantization methods degrade local texture in SR-specific ways, motivating the need for a tailored approach.

The technical components are reasonably well-motivated: H-SVD is grounded in the empirical observation (Fig. 4) that top PCs dominate SR quality but standard SVD-G alone doesn't capture fine local structure; VaSMP is derived from a clean rate-distortion argument with empirical support (Fig. 5 showing stable within-layer, diverse across-layer variance); VaTMP is similarly grounded in a variance-based distortion model and solved efficiently via DP.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four real-world benchmarks, two bit-width settings (W4A6/W4A4), and comparisons against a large and current set of baselines (including ICML/ICCV/CVPR 2025 methods), with consistent SOTA results in both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual comparisons (Fig. 7).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (H-SVD rank, VaSMP vs naive MP, VaTMP), plus additional analyses of practical runtime/memory, generalization to a second DiT backbone (DreamClear), calibration robustness, and an ROI-based artifact analysis — this depth of validation is notable and strengthens confidence in the claims.

Honest treatment of limitations, including the gap between theoretical and measured speedup, lack of native arbitrary-precision kernels, and residual artifacts on thin/repetitive/high-contrast textures under W4A4.

The paper acknowledges a metric-quality mismatch (e.g., Q-Diffusion/EfficientDM scoring highly on MANIQA despite visibly poor quality) rather than cherry-picking favorable metrics, which reflects intellectual honesty.
weaknesses: The VaSMP and VaTMP derivations rely on strong simplifying assumptions (per-token/per-channel Gaussianity after Hadamard transform, high-rate quantization approximation, independence across layers/timesteps for additive distortion). While empirically supported to a degree (Figs. 5-6), the paper does not rigorously validate the Gaussianity assumption itself or discuss failure modes when it breaks down (e.g., for outlier-heavy layers).

Several MUSIQ/MANIQA/ClipIQA gains over FP (e.g., DrealSR/RealSR W4A6, Table 1a) are counterintuitive (quantized model outperforming FP), which the paper attributes post hoc to quantization acting as a 'perceptual regularizer' — this explanation is plausible but not rigorously tested, and raises questions about whether some reported 'SOTA' gains reflect genuine detail preservation or metric artifacts.

The comparison baselines, while numerous, are all generic PTQ methods retrofitted to this backbone; it is unclear how much of the H-SVD/VaSMP/VaTMP benefit is specific to DiT4SR's particular architecture versus a broader class of DiT-SR models — the single additional backbone (DreamClear) generalization test is useful but limited, and only reports W4A6/W4A4 aggregate numbers without ablating why gains might differ.

The end-to-end speedup (4.51x) falls noticeably short of the theoretical operation reduction (6.14x) due to non-quantized components becoming the bottleneck, and no native low-bit kernel support exists yet — this practical gap somewhat undercuts the efficiency motivation central to the paper's framing.

Reproducibility is not fully verifiable from the text alone: exact hyperparameters (Btarget, block sizes so/si search space and final selection, DP segment discretization bounds) are described at a high level in the method but concrete values used in the main experiments (beyond SVD-L rank=8) are not clearly consolidated in one place, and code is only promised ('will be available'), not yet released.

The paper's H-SVD forward computation (Eq. 11) adds a quantized correction term as well as FP local/global branches, increasing implementation complexity; the runtime/memory analysis (Table 5, 6) shows the SVD-L Triton kernel overhead is modest, but no ablation is given for how sensitive results are to the block size search procedure across different backbones/layers, making it hard to judge robustness of the H-SVD design choices in general.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a well-motivated, underexplored problem: existing PTQ methods for diffusion models are largely designed for U-Net or generic text-to-image DiTs, and the paper shows convincingly (Fig. 1, 2, Table 1) that naively applying them to DiT-based Real-ISR causes severe texture degradation.

The three proposed components are individually well-motivated with clear theoretical grounding: H-SVD is justified by a PCA analysis showing that a small number of principal components dominate SR quality (Fig. 4); VaSMP is derived from a rate-distortion argument (Eq. 12-16) connecting output-channel variance to layer-wise quantization distortion; VaTMP extends this idea temporally with a DP-based scheduling formulation (Eq. 17-23).

Strong and consistent empirical results across four real-world benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250) and two aggressive bit-width settings (W4A6, W4A4), outperforming ten competitive baselines spanning diffusion PTQ, DiT-specific PTQ, and SR-specific PTQ methods.

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4, Fig. 8-9) isolate the contribution of each component (SVD-L rank, VaSMP vs. naive MSE-based mixed precision, VaTMP scheduling), providing good evidence that each piece contributes non-trivially and that a naive alternative (global MSE-based mixed precision) underperforms the variance-aware design.

Notably efficient calibration requirements: VaSMP is entirely data-free/offline, and VaTMP needs only 32 LR calibration images, making the approach attractive relative to methods requiring extensive calibration data or iterative optimization.
Reports concrete efficiency gains (5.8x model size reduction, 6.14x operation reduction under W4A4) alongside quality metrics, situating the compression-quality trade-off clearly.
weaknesses: No actual wall-clock inference latency or throughput measurements are reported; only parameter counts and FLOPs are given. Since the method uses fine-grained, irregular per-layer and per-timestep bit-widths (e.g., 3/4/5-bit mixes shown in Fig. 3, 6, 9), it is unclear whether these theoretical FLOP savings translate into real hardware speedups given the lack of efficient low-bit kernels supporting such heterogeneous configurations. This is an important gap for a paper motivated by "real-world deployment."

All experiments use a single backbone (DiT4SR); no results are shown on other DiT-based SR architectures (e.g., DreamClear) to demonstrate that H-SVD/VaSMP/VaTMP generalize beyond one specific model, which is important given the framework's claim of being broadly tailored to "DiT-based Real-ISR."

Some baseline numbers look implausibly poor and are not scrutinized (e.g., QueST attains LIQE scores near 1.0-1.15, far below even the naive Q-Diffusion baseline, across essentially all datasets and both bit-width settings), raising a question about whether baselines were properly tuned/reproduced for this specific SR setting versus their original text-to-image use cases; this could inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

No variance/standard deviation or multiple-run statistics are reported for any quantitative result, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (often modest, e.g., MUSIQ 67.51→67.72) improvements over the second-best method (SVDQuant) under W4A6.

The interaction between VaSMP (weight bit allocation) and VaTMP (activation bit allocation) is handled sequentially/greedily (weights fixed first, then activations optimized), with no analysis of whether joint optimization would yield further gains, nor a discussion of why sequential greedy allocation is near-optimal.

Sensitivity to the size/composition of the 32-image calibration set for VaTMP is not studied; given that timestep-wise activation variance statistics are collected from this small set, it would strengthen the paper to show robustness across different calibration set choices/sizes.

Limited discussion of failure cases or scenarios where H-SVD/VaSMP/VaTMP might not help (e.g., extremely low bit-widths beyond W4A4, or content types with atypical high-frequency statistics), and no explicit limitations section despite space likely being available.
